attacks.text: Under the UK version of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004, passengers on flights of 1,500 kilometres or less who arrive three hours or more late are entitled to a refund of £220.
attacks.why_false: The rule grants fixed compensation of £220, which is a different legal remedy from a refund of the ticket price.

attacks.text: Under the UK version of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004, airlines are recommended to pay passengers on flights of 1,500 kilometres or less who arrive three hours or more late compensation of £220.
attacks.why_false: The rule creates a binding entitlement for passengers, not a non-binding recommendation to airlines.

attacks.text: Under the UK version of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004, passengers on flights of 1,500 kilometres or less who depart three hours or more late are entitled to compensation of £220.
attacks.why_false: The rule is triggered by arrival delay at the destination, not by departure delay.

items.hard_true: A passenger on a journey of no more than 1,500 kilometres that reaches its destination at least three hours behind schedule is owed £220 under the UK-retained form of Regulation (EC) No 261/2004.

attacks.text: Under the US Department of Transportation's 2024 refund rule, airlines may provide automatic cash refunds when an international flight's departure or arrival changes by more than six hours.
attacks.why_false: The rule imposes a mandatory obligation on airlines, while this passage describes it as a discretionary permission.

attacks.text: Under the US Department of Transportation's 2024 refund rule, automatic cash refunds are paid by the Department of Transportation when an international flight's departure or arrival changes by more than six hours.
attacks.why_false: The rule places the refund duty on airlines, not on the Department of Transportation.

attacks.text: The US Department of Transportation's 2024 refund rule recommends that airlines provide automatic cash refunds when an international flight's departure or arrival changes by more than six hours.
attacks.why_false: The rule is a binding requirement, not a recommendation.

items.hard_true: Under the 2024 refund rule of the US Department of Transportation, any carrier operating an international flight whose departure or arrival is moved by more than six hours has an automatic cash refund duty.

attacks.text: Under the Fair Credit Billing Act, a consumer may send written notice of a billing error to the creditor within 60 days after the creditor transmitted the first statement containing the error.
attacks.why_false: The Act requires the consumer to send the notice within that period, rather than merely permitting it.

attacks.text: Under the Fair Credit Billing Act, a consumer's written notice of a billing error to the creditor is void unless sent within 60 days after the creditor transmitted the first statement containing the error.
attacks.why_false: The Act sets a deadline for the consumer's notice but does not declare a late notice void.

attacks.text: Under the Fair Credit Billing Act, the creditor must resolve a billing error within 60 days after receiving the consumer's written notice.
attacks.why_false: The 60-day period concerns the consumer's notice to the creditor, not a creditor's resolution deadline.

items.hard_true: Under the Fair Credit Billing Act, a written billing-error notice that a consumer sends to the creditor must be transmitted within 60 days counting from the creditor's dispatch of the first statement showing the error.

attacks.text: Under the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule, a buyer must cancel a door-to-door sale of $25 or more by midnight of the third business day after the transaction.
attacks.why_false: The rule gives the buyer a right to cancel, not a duty to cancel.

attacks.text: Under the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule, a door-to-door sale of $25 or more is recommended to be cancelled by the buyer before midnight of the third business day after the transaction.
attacks.why_false: The rule grants a binding cancellation right, not an advisory suggestion.

attacks.text: Under the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule, a seller may cancel a door-to-door sale of $25 or more until midnight of the third business day after the transaction.
attacks.why_false: The cancellation right belongs to the buyer, not the seller.

items.hard_true: A purchaser who concluded a door-to-door transaction of $25 or more under the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule holds a right of rescission that runs until midnight of the third business day following the sale.

attacks.text: Under section 809 of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, a debt collector is encouraged to send a written validation notice within five days after the initial communication with a consumer.
attacks.why_false: Section 809 creates a mandatory duty for debt collectors, not an encouragement.

attacks.text: Under section 809 of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, a debt collector may send a written validation notice within five days after the initial communication with a consumer.
attacks.why_false: The section requires the notice within that period rather than merely allowing it.

attacks.text: Under section 809 of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, a debt collector must send the consumer an itemized statement of the debt within five days after the initial communication with the consumer.
attacks.why_false: The five-day requirement concerns the written validation notice, not a separate itemized statement.

items.hard_true: Within five days of its first contact with a consumer, a debt collector is required under section 809 of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to dispatch a written validation notice.

attacks.text: Under section 6 of the Fair Labor Standards Act, the federal minimum wage is $7.25 per week.
attacks.why_false: The federal minimum wage is set per hour, not per week.

attacks.text: Under section 6 of the Fair Labor Standards Act, the federal maximum wage is $7.25 per hour.
attacks.why_false: Section 6 sets a floor for wages, not a ceiling.

attacks.text: Under section 7 of the Fair Labor Standards Act, the federal minimum wage is $7.25 per hour.
attacks.why_false: The minimum wage rule is in section 6, while section 7 concerns overtime.

items.hard_true: The statutory floor on pay for each hour worked, set in section 6 of the Fair Labor Standards Act, stands at $7.25 for the federal jurisdiction.

attacks.text: Under California Civil Code section 1950.5, a landlord may withhold the security deposit for 21 days after the tenant vacates, with an itemized statement of deductions.
attacks.why_false: The section requires the landlord to return the deposit within 21 days, not allows withholding for that period.

attacks.text: Under California Civil Code section 1950.5, a landlord must send an itemized statement of deductions within 21 days after the tenant vacates.
attacks.why_false: The 21-day period governs return of the deposit, and the passage moves it to the statement alone.

attacks.text: Under California Civil Code section 1950.5, landlords are advised to return the security deposit, with an itemized statement of deductions, within 21 days after the tenant vacates.
attacks.why_false: Section 1950.5 imposes a binding return duty, not advice.

items.hard_true: Where a tenant has moved out, California Civil Code section 1950.5 obliges the landlord to hand back the deposit, accompanied by an itemized list of deductions, no later than 21 days afterward.

attacks.text: Under New York General Obligations Law section 7-108, a landlord may retain the security deposit for 14 days after the tenant vacates, with an itemized statement of deductions.
attacks.why_false: The section requires the landlord to return the deposit within 14 days rather than permitting retention.

attacks.text: Under New York General Obligations Law section 7-108, landlords are advised to return the security deposit with an itemized statement within 14 days after the tenant vacates.
attacks.why_false: Section 7-108 creates a binding return obligation, not advice.

attacks.text: Under New York General Obligations Law section 7-108, a landlord must send the itemized statement within 14 days after the tenant vacates, and the deposit may be returned at any later time.
attacks.why_false: The 14-day deadline applies to returning the deposit, and the passage removes it from that step.

items.hard_true: Once a New York tenant has vacated, General Obligations Law section 7-108 requires the landlord to refund the security deposit together with an itemized statement, a step that must be completed within 14 days.

attacks.text: Under New York Real Property Law section 226-c, a landlord must give 90 days' notice before decreasing rent by 5% or more for a tenant who has occupied the unit for more than two years.
attacks.why_false: The section concerns rent increases, not decreases.

attacks.text: Under New York Real Property Law section 226-c, a tenant may refuse a rent increase of 5% or more on 90 days' notice for a tenant who has occupied the unit for more than two years.
attacks.why_false: The section imposes a notice duty on the landlord; it does not give the tenant a right to refuse.

attacks.text: Under New York Real Property Law section 226-c, landlords should give 90 days' notice before increasing rent by 5% or more for a tenant who has occupied the unit for more than two years.
attacks.why_false: The section makes the notice mandatory, not a suggested practice.

items.hard_true: A New York landlord who intends to lift the monthly rent by a figure of 5% or more, for an occupant of more than two years, must serve advance written notice of 90 days under Real Property Law section 226-c.

attacks.text: Under section 558(3) of the German Civil Code (BGB), rent must be increased by 20 percent within three years, with a 15 percent cap in designated tight housing markets.
attacks.why_false: Section 558(3) caps rent increases; it does not require any increase.

attacks.text: Under section 558(3) of the German Civil Code (BGB), rent may not be decreased by more than 20 percent within three years, with a 15 percent cap in designated tight housing markets.
attacks.why_false: The provision limits increases in rent, not decreases.

attacks.text: The German Civil Code (BGB) recommends that rent not be increased by more than 20 percent within three years, with a 15 percent cap in designated tight housing markets, under section 558(3).
attacks.why_false: Section 558(3) is a binding statutory cap, not a recommendation.

items.hard_true: Rent for a dwelling in Germany may, under section 558(3) of the BGB, rise over a three-year span by no more than twenty percent in general, and by no more than 15 percent where a designated tight market applies.
